vignette:
He is a 41-year-old South Asian man who works as an architect, and when he first begins talking about what happened, he does it the way he describes difficult building sites: carefully, with measurements, sequence, and structure. He says that in the beginning his marriage looked solid from the outside. He and his wife are both accomplished, admired by relatives, busy enough that other people mistake their exhaustion for success. He spends long days at his firm reviewing elevations, correcting drafts, and sitting with clients who want homes that feel open and calm. He has always taken pride in making spaces that hold people gently. It is hard for him to admit that his own home has come to feel dangerous.

He says the first time she hit him, he did not even call it that. They are arguing late at night about money and about his long hours. She throws a glass that shatters against the wall near his head. Then she shoves him hard in the chest. He is stunned less by the force than by the impossibility of it. He tells himself she is under strain. He cleans up the glass before bed so no one gets cut in the morning. The next day he goes to work with a tightness in his shoulders and spends an hour redrawing a stair detail because he cannot hold his attention steady.

Over the next months, the violence becomes part of the rhythm of the household, though he keeps trying to deny the pattern. She slaps him during arguments, digs her nails into his forearm, once corners him in the kitchen and hits him repeatedly with both fists while accusing him of humiliating her. He does not hit back. He is bigger than she is, and that fact becomes its own prison; he is terrified that if he defends himself, even by restraining her, he will be seen as the aggressor. He grows skilled at reading tiny changes in her face the way he reads stress lines in a structure—jaw tightening, footsteps quickening, a cabinet door closed just a little too hard. His body starts reacting before his mind catches up. His stomach drops when he hears keys in the front door. His heart pounds when her voice sharpens from another room.

The worst incident happens after a family gathering. In front of relatives, she is charming and warm. On the drive home she is silent, and he knows from the pressure in the car that something is coming. Inside the house she accuses him of siding with his parents against her. He tries to walk away, but she follows him into the bedroom, throws his phone, and strikes him across the face with a metal picture frame. He remembers the strange brightness of the room after that, the blood on his shirt, the ringing in his ears. More than the pain, what stays with him is the humiliation of kneeling on the floor, trying to gather the broken pieces before anyone sees, as if tidiness might restore dignity. He tells an urgent care clinician that he slipped into a shelf. He hears himself lie in a calm voice and feels split in two while saying it.

After that, his world begins to narrow. He sleeps lightly, waking at the smallest noise. If she turns in bed too suddenly, he is instantly alert, breath held, muscles rigid. He has dreams in which he is trapped inside one of his own buildings, every corridor leading back to the same locked room. During the day, images from the assaults break into his mind without warning: her raised hand, the glint of the frame, the sound of glass. At work he becomes ashamed of how often he startles. A junior colleague drops a roll of plans on the conference table and he flinches so visibly that everyone looks up. He begins avoiding site visits where there is shouting or banging. He stays late at the office, not because he is more productive, but because the hours before going home fill him with dread.

He tells no one for a long time. In his family and community, he has absorbed the idea that men are supposed to endure, provide, and keep private matters private. He imagines the disbelief he would meet if he said aloud that he is afraid of his wife. That disbelief becomes part of the trauma. He grows distant from friends. When his brother asks why he never comes by anymore, he says deadlines are crushing him. His wife sometimes apologizes tearfully after an incident, and those moments leave him almost more disoriented than the assaults. He starts doubting his memory, replaying arguments to see whether he caused them, whether he is too cold, too absent, too provoking without meaning to be.

Now, even in rooms where no threat exists, he scans for exits automatically. He chooses chairs with a clear line to the door. Sudden movement beside him sends heat through his chest. He has become irritable in ways that trouble him; he snaps at coworkers over minor revisions, then sits alone feeling hollow and ashamed. At home he moves quietly, trying not to create friction, trying to predict weather inside another person. He says he misses the version of himself who could imagine space as possibility. Lately every enclosed room feels like a calculation of risk. He still goes to work, still attends meetings, still answers client emails with professional precision, but underneath it he is exhausted, watchful, and never fully convinced that he is safe.
